name: Absolute Monarchism
summary: Absolute monarchism holds that all sovereign power belongs to one hereditary monarch who answers to no human body, legislature or constitution, only to God. In its classic divine-right form the king is God's lieutenant, subjects owe obedience and may not resist, and the king rules as father of his people through a centralised state, army and church.
scope: The classic early-modern European doctrine of absolutism and divine right (c. 1600 to 1789), as set out by Bossuet, James VI and I, Filmer and the practice of Louis XIV and similar rulers, with notes where modern Gulf monarchies would differ. Excludes constitutional monarchy and modern hereditary dictatorships.

sources.usedFor: Centralisation, standing armies and bureaucracy, mercantilism, nobility, church integration, enlightened absolutism.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Absolutist rulers sometimes funded hospitals and poor relief as royal paternalism, but nothing in the doctrine addresses universal state healthcare, so this is inferred and adherents would split.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Early-modern absolutist economies ran on guild and royal wage regulation, not statutory minimum wages; inferred from mercantilist state management and a hierarchical social order, so low confidence.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Absolutist states were mercantilist, with the crown directing economic activity for state strength, so adherents would not trust free markets over royal direction.

public-ownership.rationale: Crown monopolies and royal manufactories existed under absolutism, but the crown also relied on private and noble property; the doctrine has no stance on modern utilities, so adherents could go either way.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The monarch claims the right to tax at will, yet absolutist crowns notoriously spared the nobility and clergy; inferred as a mild disagreement with a push to tax the wealthy heavily.

unions-good.rationale: Absolutism dissolved or subordinated corporate bodies and rival centres of authority, and monarchs controlled guilds, so independent labour unions would be viewed as unwelcome.

property-fundamental.rationale: Absolutists held that the king may override private rights for the state, yet they also defended hereditary property and order; adherents are split on how inviolable property is.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Mercantilist crowns tightly regulated and licensed trading companies and guilds, so tighter regulation fits; inferred since modern corporations were not discussed.

cut-welfare.rationale: Modern welfare programs were not part of absolutist doctrine; paternal charity was valued while dependency arguments were not made, so the answer is inferred and split.

worker-ownership.rationale: A society of ordered estates under the king leaves no place for collective worker ownership; the idea is foreign to the doctrine and rejected by implication.

surveillance-ok.rationale: A ruler answerable only to God and responsible for order would accept extensive state watchfulness, including royal police; inferred as modern terrorism is anachronistic.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Paternalist moral government under a Christian king favours restricting vice; inferred as the doctrine does not address drug policy.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Absolutist crowns censored speech that threatened throne or church, but 'hate speech' as a category is modern; adherents could treat it either way.

strong-leader.rationale: The doctrine holds that all power should be concentrated in one sovereign who bypasses any rival body, which is exactly what this statement endorses.

state-harmful.rationale: Absolutists see royal authority as God-ordained and necessary to order, the opposite of regarding the state as unnecessary and harmful.

limit-guns.rationale: Absolutist states sought a royal monopoly on force and disarmed nobles, but modern gun-control policy is not a doctrinal matter; inferred and split.

empower-police-military.rationale: Standing armies and a loyal bureaucracy were central instruments of absolutism, so adherents favour a well-resourced military and police under the crown.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: A Christian paternalist monarchy would regulate or suppress it as a moral matter; inferred, since the topic is not addressed in the doctrine.

decide-locally.rationale: Absolutism meant centralisation: feudal partition was ended and officials answering to the crown governed localities, so local decision-making against the centre is rejected.

rehabilitation.rationale: Royal justice stressed punishment and deterrence in the monarch's name, with the king as supreme judge; inferred disagreement, though some enlightened absolutists reformed prisons.

traditional-family.rationale: Bossuet grounds royal authority in paternal authority and the family, so adherents see traditional family order as foundational to society.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: A throne-and-altar order built on Christian morality and the paternal family would reject it, though the topic is anachronistic and inferred.

abortion-legal.rationale: A Christian monarchy defending the established church's morality would oppose abortion; inferred from religious grounding rather than a stated position.

more-religion-public.rationale: Divine right ties the crown to God and the established church, so religion has a large place in public life.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The question is anachronistic for the doctrine; inferred opposition from its view of fixed hierarchical order and royal prerogative over social programs.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Gender roles in absolutist thought rested on divine and natural order, patriarchal authority and male succession; inferred since the doctrine never addressed the idea.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Absolutist monarchs promoted unified state laws, language and court culture centred on the crown, so preserving tradition is valued.

gradual-change.rationale: Adherents defend inherited institutions and the throne as providentially ordained, so change should be slow and respect established order, though the king may reform by decree.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Absolutist states often welcomed useful immigrants (Huguenots in Prussia) and excluded others; no single doctrinal line, so adherents split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: A sovereign who answers to no earthly authority rejects supranational bodies holding power over the realm.

free-trade.rationale: Absolutist economies were mercantilist and protectionist, aiming at state strength and trade surpluses rather than open trade.

nation-first.rationale: Absolutism rests on sovereign independence of the crown and mercantilist state-building for the realm's strength, over cooperation that binds the sovereign.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The modern human-rights framing is anachronistic; absolutist sovereignty implies non-interference in other crowns' realms, though dynastic and religious interventions occurred.

open-borders.rationale: A territorial sovereign controlling subjects and trade under mercantilism has no place for open borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Mercantilist absolutism prized growth in wealth for state power; environmental limits are anachronistic, so inferred disagreement.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Modern topic; a sovereign with unchecked power could impose measures, but nothing in the doctrine bears on it, so it is neutral.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Enlightened absolutists promoted science and reform, but no doctrinal view on technological salvation exists; inferred and split.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine is silent, and adherents today could favour it for state strength or oppose it for other reasons.

revolution-justified.rationale: Bossuet holds the king's person inviolable and attacking him sacrilege; divine right treats resistance and deposition as contrary to God's will.

experts-over-public.rationale: Absolutism relied on officials dependent on the crown rather than popular input, and enlightened absolutists proclaimed 'everything for the people, nothing by the people'.

central-planning.rationale: Mercantilist crowns directed the economy heavily but not through comprehensive planning; the comparison is anachronistic, so mild and low confidence.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not a doctrinal matter; adherents would prefer hierarchy and property under royal authority to workers' or public ownership of firms.

land-value-tax.rationale: A fiscal reform idea unrelated to absolutist doctrine, though the crown claims the right to tax as it chooses; neutral inference.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Absolutist order rested on hereditary families and aristocracy, so heavy inheritance taxes would clash with it; inferred.

basic-income.rationale: A modern programme absent from the doctrine; royal paternal charity is conditional on loyalty and order, so mild disagreement inferred.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Mercantilism, the characteristic economic policy of absolutist states, used tariffs and state-backed manufactures to build national wealth.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Absolutist crowns founded royal manufactories and chartered monopolies to serve state power, consistent with directing investment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Absolutism did not aim at spreading property widely; some monarchs protected peasants against nobles, others favoured landed elites, so adherents split.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The idea belongs to communism and contradicts a hierarchical monarchical order with money, taxation and royal revenues.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Anachronistic; but a sovereign who controls coinage and finance would not leave money to the market.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Guilds and estates under royal control resemble state-recognised bodies, but joint price-setting is a later corporatist idea, so inferred.

one-party-rule.rationale: Absolute monarchy is distinguished from party dictatorships; the monarch rules personally by right, not through an ideological party.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The doctrine holds hereditary monarchy to be the best and God-ordained form of government; Bossuet calls the throne the throne of God.

democracy-best.rationale: Authority comes from God through the king and subjects have no right to limit it, so democracy is not the best form even if voters choose well.

direct-votes.rationale: Legislatures were made subordinate or dissolved under absolute monarchy, and law is made by the monarch alone, so popular lawmaking is rejected.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as the basis of power contradicts sovereignty vested in the king alone.

right-to-secede.rationale: Absolutism centralised and unified the realm under one crown, ending feudal partition, so a right to secede is rejected.

natural-rulers.rationale: Divine right holds the royal dynasty is chosen by providence to rule, so some are by God's design suited to rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: Subjects may not use violence against the king, but the sovereign himself wages war and punishes by force, so the statement is rejected as universal pacifism; split on subjects' side makes it low.

war-builds-character.rationale: Absolutist rulers made war a prerogative of kings and glory of the crown, but justifying it as character-building is not a doctrinal claim.

separate-church-state.rationale: Divine right monarchs claimed religious authority and integrated the church into the state, as Henry VIII's Supreme Head of the Church.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Bossuet derived politics from Holy Scripture; yet the king as legislator makes positive law, so adherents want scripture as foundation rather than a literal code.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The king is supreme judge and holds the monopoly on force; royal justice and army are core of sovereign authority.

military-superiority.rationale: Absolutist states built standing armies and pursued dynastic glory and power, so maintaining superiority is typical, though not stated as doctrine.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Absolutist realms were dynastic and multi-ethnic (Habsburg, Russian), with loyalty owed to the crown rather than ethnic nation; inferred.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Order of estates under a paternal king is natural; class conflict as driver of history is a Marxist idea and denied by adherents.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Hierarchy of estates and privilege is part of the social order defended by absolutism, so equality of outcomes is rejected.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Anachronistic; sovereignty over all land lies with the crown, so inferred disagreement with separate authority.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Absolutist crowns built colonial empires on mercantilist principles; inferred rejection of reparations, which are a modern idea.

civilizational-union.rationale: Absolutist monarchs defended the independent sovereignty of their crown; unification above the throne is inferred as disfavoured, though dynastic unions existed.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Bossuet requires kings and subjects to act under God and duty, with humility; pursuing self-interest as such is not a moral good.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Subjects owe obedience; rights were hierarchical and few, and the only protection against authority is innocence, so duty comes first.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Not addressed; a Christian view gives nature value as God's creation but also for human use, so it is split.

limit-population.rationale: Mercantilist absolutism viewed a large population as a source of state power, so limiting growth is disfavoured; inferred.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Anachronistic; absolutist states promoted manufactures, so inferred disagreement.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Adherents prefer stability and established institutions, but enlightened absolutists promoted innovation, so low confidence disagreement.

human-enhancement.rationale: A Christian monarchical order with a fixed view of human nature would be cautious; inferred, as the topic is anachronistic.

algorithmic-government.rationale: The doctrine places authority in the person of the king; handing governing to algorithms is inferred as rejected.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A sovereign with total authority and no checks has no ground to accept secrecy from the state; inferred only.

restore-past-order.rationale: Divine-right adherents defend an order seen as providential and inherited; modern champions often look back to it, though the 17th-century doctrine was an active reformist state-building, so low.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Politics under divine right is judged by conformity to God's ordering of kingship, not by results alone; inferred.

direct-action.rationale: Resistance to the sovereign is illegitimate, and change comes by the king's decree rather than popular action outside institutions.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Absolutist states built bureaucracies, armies and manufactures; a return to foraging is foreign to the doctrine.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: An ordered hierarchy of estates with distinct functions is the natural order for absolutists.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distribution by rank, privilege and royal favour, not need, characterised the absolutist order.

production-for-use.rationale: Mercantilism prized profit and trade surpluses for the state; inferred disagreement with production for use.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Marxist exploitation theory is foreign to absolutism, which defended property and the existing social order.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The monarch alone holds sovereign power over all classes, so class dictatorship is rejected.

collective-farming.rationale: Absolutist agriculture rested on noble and peasant landholding, so collective farming is rejected.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Marxist analysis is rejected; absolutists attribute war to dynastic and state rivalry, but the statement is not directly addressed.

taxation-theft.rationale: The monarch is sole lawgiver with the right to levy taxes without consent; taxation is a legitimate royal power.

harm-principle.rationale: The sovereign is above human law and the state governs morals and religion, so restricting only harm to others is rejected.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Rights in this order were hierarchical and tied to status, estates and corporate bodies, not held by individuals alone.

conscription.rationale: Standing armies and royal authority over subjects mean a monarch may compel service; absolutist states used levies and recruitment.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Subjects owe obedience to the crown; neither voting nor exit is a legitimate check on the sovereign.

state-as-business.rationale: The king is God's lieutenant and father of his people, not a business manager with customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Liberty in this tradition is obedience to law under a just king; material means for freedom is not a doctrinal concern, so inferred.

media-academia-power.rationale: Anachronistic; no doctrinal position, though modern adherents may resent elites.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Racial genetics is not part of the doctrine; its hereditary principle is dynastic, so inferred disagreement with low confidence.

organic-representation.rationale: Estates and corporate bodies as representation under the crown was the historic pattern, but absolutism subordinated them, so inferred and low.

total-state.rationale: Absolutism claims all political power but pre-modern states lacked capacity for total control; Bossuet distinguishes absolute from arbitrary, so mild disagreement.

national-rebirth.rationale: Absolutists defend providential continuity of the crown rather than radical rebirth, an ideal of modern revolutionary movements.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Dynastic expansion and wars of conquest were characteristic of absolutist monarchs such as Louis XIV and Frederick the Great.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Absolutism replaced feudal oaths of lords with centralised royal authority, but loyalty to the person of the king remained central; the statement reads as feudal, so split.

bound-labor.rationale: Serfdom persisted under many absolutists (Russia) while others such as Joseph II abolished it, so adherents split.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Knowledge in this tradition is anchored in revelation and reason, not in power, so rejected; inferred.

universal-morality.rationale: Bossuet draws politics from scripture and natural and divine law binding all, implying universal moral truths, though mostly through faith.

single-common-good.rationale: The king gathers the whole people into one person and rules for the common good; no balancing of groups.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not addressed by absolutist doctrine; split.

revive-national-language.rationale: Not a doctrinal issue; absolutist states did standardise official languages but revival is not addressed.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Hierarchy and authority of owner and crown over estates, not democratic vote in firms.

school-vouchers.rationale: Absolutist states favoured church or crown-controlled education; inferred.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Royal finances ran in perpetual difficulty; no doctrinal view on stimulus.

economic-freedom.rationale: Absolutists held political order comes first and economies served the state; they would not accept that political freedom depends on economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Bossuet stresses the king's duty to rule with humility and fear of God and the majesty that images God; yet laws and punishments also matter, so only partial agreement.

national-self-determination.rationale: Dynastic rule over many peoples and legitimacy through inheritance, not nation, is the absolutist principle.

force-without-un.rationale: Sovereigns decide war themselves without external approval; the UN is anachronistic, so inferred.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Divine right rests on revealed faith and scripture, so reason alone is not the only guide.

class-collaboration.rationale: The social order of estates under the king is supposed to be harmonious, with each serving its function, so cooperation is preferred to class war.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Royal institutions, libraries and court culture were patronised as monarchy's glory; adherents would reject sacrificing heritage.

workers-nation.rationale: Workers' organisation is not a category in this order, and national labour classes would be rejected as political actors.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Patriarchal order and male succession in most absolutist monarchies, with law reflecting distinct roles.

ban-interest.rationale: Church condemned usury, but absolutist states relied on credit and tolerated interest; inferred with low confidence.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; legal order was by estates and subject status, not race, though colonial codes existed.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Absolutists see the state as God-ordained and the king as father of all, not an instrument of a class.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Established-church monarchies enforced religious uniformity (Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes); inferred as typical though not explicit.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: A modern energy question absent from the doctrine; mercantilist concern for national self-sufficiency pulls one way, nothing else bears on it.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Absolutist states pursued unified laws and religion within the realm (Huguenots were pressed to convert), so inferred support for assimilation, though not stated as doctrine.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory about replacement has no place in the doctrine and is not asserted by its sources; adherents hold that order comes from the crown.

proportional-representation.rationale: Legislatures are subordinate or dissolved under absolute monarchy, so allocating seats by party vote is not part of the order.

national-mission.rationale: Some monarchs saw a providential mission for their dynasty or faith, but spreading a form of government is not a doctrinal claim.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Adherents would defend male authority as the natural order rather than call it a system that advantages men, but would not deny men hold it; split on framing.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Absolutists blamed rival nobles and parliaments for faction, not the royal government, though court intrigue was recognised; inferred.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics is a modern programme not found in the doctrine; the Christian paternal monarchy would not favour it, though inferred.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The king is answerable only to God and his forces act in his name, so legal accountability for the crown's security forces is rejected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Absolutist government regulated religion, economy and morals under mercantilism, far beyond a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Not a doctrinal matter; dynastic marriage practice was about rank and religion, not race.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Souls are equal before God but rights were hierarchical and unequal by estate under the king, so equal rights before the law are rejected.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist question foreign to monarchy; adherents reject socialism, so the premise is rejected, with low interest.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Absolutist monarchies founded settler colonies as royal projects, so they would not accept the framing; inferred.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Absolutist states unified law within the realm, but religious law for subjects (Ottoman millets, church courts) also persisted, so split.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not part of European absolutism and not a doctrinal matter; mild disagreement inferred.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Established church and monarchy were intertwined, with religious instruction in royal and state schools.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist formulation; adherents would affirm a strong state but the statement is about socialism, so neutral.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Authority comes from God and subjects have no right to limit it, so authority does not rest on consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilism, the economic policy of absolutist states, aimed at export surpluses to build state treasuries.

population-transfer.rationale: Absolutist crowns expelled minorities such as the Huguenots and Moriscos, but the statement is not a doctrine and adherents split.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The sovereign wages war and enforces his law by right; libertarian non-aggression is incompatible with that.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Not a doctrinal claim; inter-state rivalry drove absolutist state-building but order is prized over struggle.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: A sovereign who dissolves councils and bans parties (as in Saudi Arabia and Oman) accepts suppressing parties; inferred as the constitutional order is the crown.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Bossuet holds royal power is absolute and subjects' only protection is their innocence, which is the arbitrary-power condition this republican view denies as freedom; though he distinguishes absolute from arbitrary.

separated-powers.rationale: The king concentrates legislative, executive and judicial authority in one person, so division among checking bodies is rejected.

vanguard-party.rationale: A revolutionary party is foreign to monarchy; adherents reject revolution and party rule.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Christian kings had duties of charity to the poor, but laws giving first priority to the poor are not stated, so split.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Crowns controlled guilds and prohibited combinations of workers; inferred support for restricting strikes.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Mercantilist absolutists saw large populations as a strength, so they would not blame population; inferred.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The rulers pursued religious and legal uniformity in the realm to secure unity, so inferred agreement.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices are filled by royal appointment and by hereditary right, and the king is not elected or random.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: A sovereign above human law may suspend any legal protections in emergency, as the monarch makes and annuls laws.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Mercantilist and paternal crowns regulated grain and bread prices in scarcity as part of their duty to subjects.

party-controls-media.rationale: Absolutist crowns licensed and censored print; media control by the ruling party is not their model, so split in wording.

party-commands-army.rationale: The army is commanded by the monarch personally, not by a party.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Not a doctrinal matter; citizenship was subject status under the crown.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: No elected representatives with real power exist in the order, so the demand is foreign; inferred.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The sovereign answers to no earthly authority and so cannot share sovereignty with a supranational body.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The monarch commands the army and names ministers, as in the French and Prussian absolutist states.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Monarchies with established churches (Catholic and Anglican) were governed by bishops under the crown, as James I held 'no bishop, no king'; inferred.

clerical-rule.rationale: Divine right holds the king, not the clergy, rules; pope and bishops are subordinate in secular affairs.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Subjects owe obedience and loyalty to the king, especially in war.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Absolutist and Counter-Reformation monarchies licensed and censored works for religious and moral reasons.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The ruler holds office for life by inheritance, so the question is not apt; neutral.

recall-officials.rationale: Subjects have no power over the king, and officials serve at the king's pleasure, not the voters'.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Absolutist monarchs made dynastic alliances and wars freely; withdrawing is not their stance, but low confidence.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Landed property and rent were basic to the order; abolishing them is rejected.

people-in-arms.rationale: Absolutism relied on professional standing armies dependent on the crown; an armed citizenry would threaten royal monopoly of force.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Landed aristocracy and peasants were the base of the old order, but the court and cities were also central; split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Dynastic rather than national logic governed borders in absolutism; neutral.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Not a doctrinal matter; kings used educated officials, so split.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Adherents hold their own Christian monarchic order to be proper and divinely sanctioned; inferred.

death-penalty.rationale: The king is supreme judge who can impose death sentences without appeal, and monarchs used capital punishment freely.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Christian morality under the established church would reject it; inferred since the topic is modern.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Scripture grounds the doctrine, so adherents lean towards teaching creation, but the evolution debate is modern; inferred.

restrict-pornography.rationale: A paternal Christian monarchy regulated public morals, and censored obscenity.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Allegiance in monarchy passes by lineage and birth under the crown; inferred as the doctrine does not address citizenship.

minority-language-support.rationale: Absolutist states often unified language and administration, so minority-language support is inferred as disfavoured.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Established-church monarchies enforced religious uniformity (Louis XIV ended toleration of Protestants), so exemptions are disfavoured.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conformity to custom and religion was valued; eccentricity as a good in itself is a liberal view.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: A modern question not addressed; neutral.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: A post-colonial argument foreign to the doctrine; rejected by inference.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The monarch is the sole source of law and the constitution; an elected assembly rewriting it is rejected.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Absolutist states restricted political freedoms and promoted economic development under mercantilism.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Christian charity is valued, but state duties to foreign poor are not part of the doctrine; split.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Sovereign independence and military strength matter to absolutist states, but nuclear arms are anachronistic; inferred.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state is hereditary and the elective principle is rejected.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The crown controlled coinage and finance; independence from the sovereign contradicts that, inferred.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial concessions were dynastic and practical; no doctrinal line.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The king rules for the common good, and property rights can be overridden for it; Bossuet restrains kings from using power at pleasure.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A Marxist debate foreign to the doctrine; neutral.

precautionary-principle.rationale: A modern topic not addressed by the doctrine.

collective-defense.rationale: Dynastic alliances were common but a binding collective-defence rule would limit sovereign freedom, so mild agreement; inferred.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Absolutist rulers acquired territory by conquest and inheritance without popular consent, so the statement is disfavoured.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Absolutists integrated the church into the state, reducing its independent power (Gallicanism, the Supreme Head); but divine right also respects the church, so mild.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The monarch is above parties and factions and embodies the whole people, and Bossuet says he gathers all into one person.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Absolutism centralised and held the realm together under the crown, making force against secession plausible; inferred.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Absolutist states in practice kept provincial privileges (France's pays d'etats) while centralising, so adherents split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Bossuet calls the king's person sacred and the throne God's own, but divine descent is claimed only in non-Christian monarchies like the Inca; adherents split on the second half.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Modern fiscal debate not addressed; the crown taxes by decree.

character-from-environment.rationale: Adherents hold a fixed nature and lineage; heredity and rank are central, so inferred disagreement.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Denmark-Norway's 1665 law placed the monarch above all human law, answerable only to God; Bossuet says the prince answers to no earthly authority.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Absolute monarchy concentrates power in one and dissolves rival councils, so mixed rule is rejected.

leader-cult.rationale: Bossuet calls royal majesty the image of God's grandeur; honouring the king in portraits and ceremony (Versailles) was characteristic.

equal-parenting.rationale: A modern family-law issue not addressed.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Marxist internal debate foreign to monarchy; neutral to disagree.

land-redistribution.rationale: The nobility and landed order stand beside the throne; seizing estates attacks it.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Dynastic claims rather than nationality governed absolutist territorial claims, so nationality-based claim is not their basis; split.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Established-church monarchs, Catholic and Islamic, punished apostasy and heresy; inferred.

women-must-cover.rationale: Gulf monarchies require dress rules but European absolutism did not; adherents split.

common-currency.rationale: Coinage is a royal prerogative; a shared currency would pool sovereignty, so mild disagreement.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Dynastic loyalty rather than kinship drives politics; unity across borders would dissolve crowns.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Absolutism centralises authority under the crown, leaving little room for self-governing minority institutions.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Absolutist sources say nothing about minority emigration versus struggle for rights; subjects owe obedience to their own crown and no stance can be inferred.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Bossuet and divine right see history as governed by providence, not by economic conditions.

ban-cartels.rationale: Crowns granted monopolies and privileges to favoured companies, so breaking up concentrations is not their line.

no-bailouts.rationale: Royal bailouts of favoured firms and nobles is consistent with mercantilism; inferred.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Not apt to the doctrine; neutral.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Patriarchal order with male succession would reject mandated parity.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Mercantilist theory aimed at a self-sufficient empire with trade favouring the metropole.

moral-incentives.rationale: Duty and honour are central to court society but material rewards and patronage also drove loyalty; split.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Revolution is sacrilege against the sovereign in this doctrine.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hereditary monarchy and a noble order are the foundation of absolutism.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Courts promoted history glorifying dynasty and realm, so inferred agreement.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Absolutist colonial powers justified rule over other peoples by missionary and civilising claims; inferred.

patriotic-education.rationale: Loyalty to crown and realm was inculcated in schools, with royal and religious symbols; inferred.

public-money-creation.rationale: Coinage and money were royal prerogatives; a public body creating money fits, though modern banking is anachronistic.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Dynastic ambition for influence over formerly held lands fits absolutist foreign policy; inferred.

delink-world-market.rationale: Mercantilists wanted trade favourable to their state, not delinking; inferred.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Marxist concept foreign to the doctrine.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Absolutist societies were status-based and regulated associations by rank and religion, not private freedom to refuse service; inferred.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The monarch is not bound by human law, and subjects have no legal rights against him, so an entrenched bill of rights is rejected.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Absolutist theory never discusses colonial treaties, and royal powers made and broke treaties by prerogative, so there is no firm basis for a side.

elective-rulers.rationale: Absolute monarchy is hereditary and subjects cannot choose or limit the ruler.

minority-veto.rationale: The monarch decides alone and binds all subjects, so no veto is recognised.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Bossuet says only innocence protects subjects against authority; divine right treats resistance and deposition as contrary to God's will.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Under absolute monarchy legislatures are subordinate or dissolved, with the king making and annulling laws.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine; Christian views vary.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Christian tradition permits use of animals; cruelty is discouraged; inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Bossuet requires kings to rule with humility and duty, and the paternal order obliges the privileged to serve others.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Service to the king and realm is a duty and honour in the court order, so withdrawal is not endorsed.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Rule rests on divine right and royal authority, not winning consent through culture; inferred.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory is foreign and the absolutist colonial powers profited by mercantilism; rejected by inference.

native-born-offices.rationale: Absolutist monarchs often employed foreigners as officials, so split.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Dynastic wars aimed at recovering lost lands (Louis XIV's wars), so inferred support.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Sovereignty is vested in the crown; inferred rejection of leadership by descent from pre-colonial peoples.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Fascism postdates the doctrine and the sources never discuss constitutional founding values; monarchists could split on it.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Absolute monarchy is distinguished from hereditary dictatorship, and adherents oppose communism and revolutionary regimes; low confidence.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A US historiographic matter not addressed.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Defence of inherited tradition and historical figures fits; inferred.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Modern social-policy question the absolutist sources never address, so adherents are not clearly on either side.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The sources never address domestic-violence policy; a paternal order protects family members but gives no view on symmetry.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Divine right and Gulf absolutism are defended as suited to their societies, against Western democratic forms.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Absolutism relied on the army as the instrument of the crown, though political role is the king's own; inferred.

filial-duty.rationale: Bossuet grounds royal authority in paternal authority, and filial duty is the model for obedience.

office-by-exam.rationale: Offices under absolutism were by royal appointment, patronage and sale, but meritocratic bureaucrats existed (Prussia, China); split.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Mercantilist state protection of strategic industries; inferred.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Church marriage doctrine would reject unilateral no-fault divorce; inferred.

recallable-delegates.rationale: The ruler is not bound by subjects' decisions.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension systems did not exist in the period; the crown paid pensions at its pleasure, which gives no clear answer on private accounts.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Hereditary landed property was part of the order, and communal tenure is foreign to it.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Charles I ruled eleven years without Parliament; legislatures are subordinate or dissolved, and the king levies taxes himself.

single-official-language.rationale: Absolutist states promoted unified state language and law (Louis XIV's French); inferred.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Hierarchical unequal-status order rejects it; inferred.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Court luxury was praised under absolutism but moralists criticised it; split.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Monarchies funded rival states' rebels in dynastic wars; inferred.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Sovereign-prerogative great-power interventions (Holy Alliance) were practised by monarchs; inferred.

corporate-influence.rationale: Modern lobbying is anachronistic; crowns granted privileges to favoured companies while resisting rival power, so adherents are split.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Gulf monarchies and absolutist crowns restrict outside influence; inferred.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Mercantilism valued population as state strength, so incentives fit.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local limits on property purchase are not discussed; the crown and nobility held land by grant, so no inference is secure.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employer-of-last-resort policy is a modern idea; paternal crowns gave poor relief and work projects but no guarantee was claimed.

democratic-peace.rationale: Democracy promotion is not their aim; war was a royal prerogative; inferred.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Bossuet requires obedience to the king as service to God, so there is a duty to obey authority.

non-intervention.rationale: Sovereigns respected each other's crowns in principle but intervened often; split.

industrial-unions.rationale: Independent unions are not accepted in the order, and anachronistic.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Not asserted in the doctrine, though persecution of Protestants and Jews occurred; low confidence.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage is a church and state institution in this order.

public-access-to-information.rationale: State secrecy belongs to royal prerogative; a legal right to access is rejected.

local-production.rationale: Mercantilist states favoured national, not strictly local, production, and the sources do not address localism.

informal-organisation.rationale: Rejects informal political groups outside the crown's order.

religious-nation.rationale: Subjects share the king's established religion; cuius regio, eius religio.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The sovereign answers to no earthly power, so domestic law outranks international courts.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Ritual tribute systems existed in China, but the statement is not European doctrine; split.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Centralised crown revenue, not regional retention, is the absolutist model.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Property in general is private in this order, with means of production not held in common, so the statement's communal premise is rejected.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Modern public-service design is not discussed in the sources; royal and church bodies provided services in mixed ways, giving no clear answer.

religion-illusion.rationale: Divine right rests on God as source of authority, so religion as illusion is rejected.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Mercantilist order built trade but nobility looked down on capitalists; split.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Patriarchal order rejected women's equality in the first place.

socialized-care.rationale: The family under paternal authority is the base of society, so private care within families is endorsed.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language academies like the Academie francaise were royal projects but purism is not doctrinal.

treaties-binding.rationale: A sovereign above human law may not be bound by treaties with subjects, though royal treaties were honoured among crowns; inferred.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Foreign to a hierarchical crown-centred order.

majority-settlement.rationale: Settlement policy toward minority regions is not discussed as doctrine, though crowns sometimes planted settlers, so adherents are split.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Dynastic and historic claims justified territory in absolutist diplomacy.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; adherents reject it as unrelated, but low confidence.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Christian and Islamic monarchies criminalised it, and Saudi and Brunei do so today.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Absolute monarchies ban parties and dissolve rival councils (Denmark, Saudi Arabia, Oman).

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Established-church monarchs punished blasphemy and heresy, tying crown and altar.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Mercantilist colonial policy governed colonies for the metropole's benefit.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Specific to Islamic law; Muslim absolute monarchies differ.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Divine right holds rulers may not be resisted or removed by subjects, even tyrants; the statement is its opposite.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Subjects have no right to limit the monarch; popular decisions are rejected.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: A modern critical concept foreign to the doctrine.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: A patriarchal Christian or Islamic order tied to fixed natural and divine categories would reject it; inferred as the topic is anachronistic.

assisted-dying.rationale: Life is God's gift in the religious framework underpinning divine right; inferred rather than stated.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Adherents place themselves firmly in a hierarchical tradition and do not seek to combine left and right; inferred.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist claim foreign to the doctrine, which defends hierarchical order and does not regard work as alienating.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Christian European absolutists and Muslim monarchies like Saudi Arabia would split; the statement is not part of the doctrine.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Bossuet calls the throne the throne of God; divine right holds the sovereign's authority comes from God, not the people.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Established religion has a public place under divine right monarchy, so banning religious dress is disfavoured; inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: A modern employment-law issue not addressed.

social-market-economy.rationale: Absolutist economics was mercantilist and state-directed, not social-market; inferred.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Standing armies were central to absolutism, so abolishing them is rejected.

rich-first.rationale: The hierarchical order accepts that some grow rich and privileged first; inferred.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Dynastic monarchs allied and fought as their interests dictated; no doctrinal line.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Most absolute monarchies are hereditary, and Bossuet argues hereditary monarchy is the form of government best suited to a realm.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Foreign to mercantilist state finance, which relied on private banks and royal borrowing; inferred.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: A sovereign answering to no outside authority would refuse conditions imposed by lenders; anachronistic, so inferred.

property-franchise.rationale: Absolutists oppose universal franchise; where representation existed it was by estates and property, which is nearer to this statement than to equal vote.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminism is foreign to a patriarchal, hierarchical order.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept not addressed by the doctrine; rejected as foreign.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: A Marxist critique that adherents would not accept, since they censor the press; inferred.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The monarch makes and annuls laws and acts as supreme judge, though Bossuet separates absolute rule from arbitrary rule and kings issued public edicts, so split.

racial-franchise.rationale: The franchise in absolutism was not racial, since subjects have no vote at all; inferred.

online-participation.rationale: Citizens' deliberation and decision is foreign to the doctrine, which gives final decision to the king.

open-government-data.rationale: The crown's secrets are royal prerogative and the public cannot oversee the sovereign.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Established-church monarchies and Islamic monarchies regulate interfaith marriage; inferred.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; royal order discouraged popular action, though persecution of minorities occurred.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Popular bodies cannot limit or share royal authority.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Adherents defend traditional orthodoxy and the established church; inferred.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Absolutist order relied on great nobles and wealth under royal control; fear of wealth was rather of nobles' power and not liberty; inferred.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Christian or Islamic traditional values would oppose; inferred.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Religion underpins royal authority; atheism promoted by the state is the opposite.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The king as supreme judge enforces his order by force.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Absolute monarchy concentrates executive power in the crown, so sharing it among communities is rejected.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The church and local community cared for the poor in the old order, with royal paternal alms as well; inferred and split between church and crown.

term-limits.rationale: The sovereign rules for life and legislatures have no power to remove or limit him.

vote-delegation.rationale: Subjects' votes have no place in the order.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Established churches under divine right monarchs reserved offices to men; inferred.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Bossuet grounds authority in paternal authority, and the husband and father's headship is part of the order; inferred.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: No subjects vote; foreigners voting would be outside the order.

rent-control.rationale: Paternal crowns regulated prices but landed interests were also protected; split.

abolish-ip.rationale: Royal privileges and monopolies protected inventors and publishers; inferred.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Absolutist armies drilled soldiers but youth movements are a modern fascist form; neutral.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: A sovereign answering to no earthly power would not accept foreign forces on its soil, though modern Gulf monarchies host them; inferred and split.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Formal recognition of past killings is a modern practice absent from absolutist sources, so no position follows.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The aristocratic order rested on income from landed ownership and privilege.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The king holds the sword of justice and war and can impose death sentences.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Dynastic legitimacy claims an unbroken line stretching back; the crown embodies the realm's continuity.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Traditional order grounds sex differences in nature and creation.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: A fixed natural order of the sexes is assumed.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Honour for those dying for king and realm was customary, but 'martyr and saint' language belongs rather to religious causes; inferred.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Bossuet draws politics from scripture, but a cosmic struggle framing was not central to absolutist writing; split.

culture-before-state.rationale: Absolutism meant state-building first by royal power, then court culture; inferred.

god-not-male.rationale: Traditional Christian language for God as Father underpins paternal royal authority.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Scripture is the authority from which politics is drawn, not to be judged by a standard like this.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Not a doctrinal matter; absolutist crowns relied on minority financiers at times (court Jews, Huguenots), so split.

independent-unions.rationale: Crowns subordinated or dissolved independent corporate bodies and rival authorities.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: A socialist demand rejected, the premise being foreign to the order.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Municipal services were mostly under local corporations or the crown; not a doctrinal issue.

second-chamber.rationale: Absolutism does not admit a legislature with power; where councils or estates exist, they were advisory, so neutral.

municipal-property.rationale: A communal ownership scheme foreign to a hierarchical property order.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Centralised power under the crown contradicts confederal self-rule.

family-wage.rationale: Paternal order with the husband as breadwinner supports it; inferred.

anonymous-payments.rationale: A sovereign who controls coinage would be wary of untraceable payments; inferred.

online-anonymity.rationale: Absolute rulers censor and surveil dissent, so anonymity is disfavoured; inferred.

person-over-state.rationale: Subjects serve the king and realm and the king gathers the whole people into one person, so the person is subordinate to the state's ends.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Bossuet's politics drawn from scripture assumes humans are spiritual beings and that politics serves God's order.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The king can annul laws and abolish rival authorities, such as Denmark's Council of the Realm, so regional powers are revocable by the crown.

gm-crops.rationale: Genetically engineered crops are a modern technology the doctrine never touches; nothing in its principles settles the question.

dense-cities.rationale: Urban density and the environment are modern questions; the sources give no basis for choosing a side.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Not part of the doctrine, which treats subjects as a single people under the crown.

racial-pride.rationale: Not addressed; dynastic and religious pride were emphasised instead.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Absolutist monarchs fought wars of expansion for dynastic glory, such as Louis XIV and Frederick the Great.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Dynastic allegiance, not language, defined the realm; multiethnic empires such as the Habsburgs and Russia show this.

communal-electorates.rationale: Subjects do not vote for representatives with power in absolutism; estates by status was the older pattern, so inferred.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Absolutist sources never assert a partition plot, though dynastic partitions did happen; adherents are split or indifferent.

free-public-college.rationale: University funding is not addressed; kings founded and endowed universities, but tuition policy is not a doctrinal matter.

future-generations.rationale: Dynastic continuity binds the present monarch to preserve the realm for heirs; inferred.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Traditional order assigns distinct roles and virtues to women; inferred.

arms-reduction.rationale: Standing armies and military power were pillars of the state, so reduction is disfavoured.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Diplomacy was the king's secret prerogative, with secret treaties common between crowns.

capital-controls.rationale: Mercantilism controlled bullion and the flows of wealth for state power.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The crown monopolises force and disarms rival nobles; centralisation required it.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Subjects owe obedience to the king's commands; refusing orders to fight would be a sin and a crime.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Crowns regulated wages and guilds; independent bargaining is disfavoured.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Tax credits for low-paid families are a modern welfare design the doctrine does not address.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: The king is not bound by laws and sets his own finances, so legal limits on his borrowing are rejected.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Reforming international economic rules for developing countries is a modern debate outside the doctrine, so no side is clear.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Revolution against the crown is sacrilege and the state is God-ordained.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The crown directs economic life under its policies and does not allow competing systems.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Pricing ecosystems as capital is a modern economic idea absent from the sources, so no position is derivable.

sacred-nation.rationale: The kingdom is sacred through the throne's divine mandate and outlasts members; the sacredness is of the crown more than the nation, so mild.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student loans did not exist; the crown's power over finance gives no clear answer on cancelling them.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Not part of the doctrine, and centralisation under the crown is defended; inferred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Scripture-based view of fixed human nature created by God; inferred.

public-service-media.rationale: Royal censorship and control, not independent public media.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Established-church monarchs hold one true faith and enforce uniformity.

farm-price-support.rationale: Paternal and mercantilist crowns regulated grain markets and supported farmers to ensure state strength; inferred.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Military strength and sovereign independence are valued; anachronistic.

workers-own-party.rationale: Parties are banned or irrelevant under absolutism and workers' politics is foreign to it.

ban-fgm.rationale: The sources never discuss it; Christian European monarchies would not have it at issue and Gulf monarchies differ, so adherents are split.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Male-preference primogeniture and male inheritance typified absolutist societies; adherents are divided on modern equality; inferred.

one-language-many-names.rationale: A linguistic classification question the doctrine never discusses; kings promoted state languages but took no stance on names.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Tort liability for pollution is a modern libertarian-legal proposal; the sources give no basis for an absolutist answer.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Council advisory roles for notables under a king are plausible, but the king makes law alone; split.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Environmental priority against liberty is a modern conflict; absolutists give liberty little weight but say nothing on the environment.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The king as supreme judge holds final discretion, including pardon, so fixed sentences binding judges are not his way; inferred.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The unified state language is part of absolutist centralisation; inferred.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Compulsory union membership is a modern labour issue; crowns compelled guild membership but unions as such are not discussed.

voter-id.rationale: Not apt, since there are no votes.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Absolutist established churches had legal precedence in the state.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Absolute monarchy denies democracy outright, though the definition itself is not addressed.

premarital-sex.rationale: Christian and Islamic morality under the monarch would reject this; inferred.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: A ruler with unchecked power to maintain order, as in Gulf monarchies, may cut communications; inferred.

negative-income-tax.rationale: This welfare design is a modern economic proposal; the sources are silent, so the answer is neutral.

women-suffrage.rationale: Subjects of absolute monarchs have no vote or office to share; Saudi Arabia held no national elections.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Adherents regard religion as the foundation of order and morality.

race-social-construct.rationale: Scientific racial categories are not discussed in the sources; dynastic and religious status, not race, defined subjects.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Patriarchal order would not create such agencies; inferred.

homestead-ownership.rationale: The crown holds ultimate dominion over land and grants it; inferred.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: The sovereign answers to no earthly authority and rejects courts above him.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Bossuet draws politics from the very words of scripture, and divine right relies on it; literal reading is split among churches.

defend-planned-state.rationale: A Marxist-state topic opposed by monarchists.

indirect-election.rationale: Offices come by royal appointment rather than election; but some monarchies have electors; neutral.

national-church-status.rationale: Divine right monarchs headed or backed a national church, as Henry VIII did with the Supreme Head of the Church of England.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Centralisation of the realm under the crown leaves little room for territorial autonomy, though provinces kept privileges in practice.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Territory goes by dynastic right and conquest rather than popular vote.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Borders of newly independent states are a post-colonial issue the doctrine never addresses, so adherents have no common view.

simple-living.rationale: Court magnificence (Versailles) was part of royal majesty; inferred, though Christian modesty is also praised.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Settlement restriction in indigenous regions is not addressed; colonial crowns both encouraged and limited settlement, so views split.

equal-conscription.rationale: Traditional gender roles assign military service to men; inferred.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Dynastic bond to land and realm exists; the formulation is nationalist so mild; inferred.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The king as supreme judge imposes sentences in his name through justice, not summary killing, though absolute rulers used such powers; inferred and split.

close-ties-china.rationale: Alignment with China is a modern foreign-policy choice; absolutist principles do not favour either option.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Dynastic claims rather than nationality; neutral.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Land and resources are held by crown, nobles and church as hierarchical property, not by everyone equally.

self-ownership.rationale: Subjects are not self-owning against the king and owe him obedience; inferred.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Crowns taxed consumption heavily (France's gabelle) and decided taxes by decree, but cutting it is not a doctrinal matter.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Universal versus targeted spending is a modern debate; paternal charity was selective but no doctrinal view exists.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The monarch rules directly, without intermediate parties and bodies, abolishing rival centres of authority; though the court itself needs advisers.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Crowns granted monopolies and privileges to favoured businesses under mercantilism.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Established-church monarchies tied politics to a single denomination.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Enlightened absolutists promoted modernisation while keeping throne and altar, but the framing is modern; inferred.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Church marriage doctrine did not allow wives to initiate divorce; inferred.

national-resource-control.rationale: Mercantilism put wealth and resources under national, royal control.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Anachronistic; royal grants and privilege shaped property, but the doctrine does not address the justice of distributions, so inferred.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Anachronistic; mercantilist rulers taxed trade, but a transactions tax on finance is inferred and adherents would split.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine never addressed modern racial groups, so no answer can be inferred.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Law is the will of the sovereign, and subjects owe obedience even to bad rulers with no right of resistance.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine has no view on automation, so inferred from its paternalism and left split.

multipolar-world.rationale: Absolutist states competed as independent sovereigns in a balance of power; inferred, and the doctrine is about domestic rule.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Anachronistic; mercantilist absolutist states favoured national wealth over labour theory; inferred.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Bossuet ties loyalty to the realm with the king's paternal care of his people; patriotism as such is inferred.

material-over-identity.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine has no left or cultural-identity politics, so inferred and split.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Anachronistic; no communist party exists in its world, and it admits no rule except the monarch's; inferred.

missingStatements.text: A king is answerable to God alone for how he rules, and no human court may judge him.
missingStatements.rationale: Bossuet says the prince answers to no earthly authority while God will demand an account, and divine right holds only God can judge a monarch.

missingStatements.text: Subjects must obey even an unjust ruler and may not resist him.
missingStatements.rationale: Divine right treats deposing or resisting the king as contrary to God's will, and Bossuet says subjects' only protection against authority is their innocence.

notes: Modern Gulf absolute monarchies add Islamic law and consultative councils, and would answer religion statements differently. Many economic and modern-social answers are low-confidence inferences.
